## Methods

Nanobody expression and purification
The coding sequence encoding the ALFA-binding nanobody (Nb) was subcloned into the pSecTag2 vector with an N-terminal 6×His tag. For expression, Human embryonic kidney (HEK) 293F cells (Invitrogen) were cultured in Freestyle 293 medium at 37°C under 5% CO₂ in a shaking incubator at 120 r.p.m. to a density of ~2 × 10⁶ cells per milliliter before transfection with expression plasmid. For 1-liter culture, 1 mg plasmid was pre-mixed with 3 mg polyethyleneimine (PEI, Polysciences, 23966-100) in 30ml of fresh medium at room temperature for 30 minutes for transfection. After transfection, the cells were cultured at 37°C for 48 hours.

The secreted nanobody protein was purified from the culture medium using Ni-NTA affinity chromatography. After centrifugation at 4,000g for 10 minutes, the collected medium was applied to Ni-NTA resin (Thermo Fisher). After washing with washing buffer (25 mM HEPES pH 7.5, 150 mM NaCl, 20 mM imidazole), the nanobody protein was eluted with washing buffer supplemented 500 mM imidazole. The eluate was further purified by gel filtration chromatography in buffer: 25 mM HEPES pH 7.5 and 150 mM NaCl. The central fractions of monodisperse peak were collected and concentrated for later preparation of the nanobody-bound form of IPC synthase.

IPC synthase expression and purification
The codon-optimized full-length cDNA constructs of S. cerevisiae AUR1 (UniProt ID: P36107) and KEI1 (UniProt ID: Q06346) were subcloned into the pCAG vectors. A FLAG tag was fused to the C-terminus of Aur1 and the ALFA tag was inserted to replace the Kei1 loop (residues 127–131). Human embryonic kidney (HEK) 293F cells (Invitrogen) were cultured in Freestyle 293 medium at 37°C under 5% CO in a shaking incubator at 120 r.p.m. For the expression of IPC synthase, cells at a density of ~2 × 10⁶ cells per milliliter were co-transfected with AUR1 and KEI1 plasmids at a 1:1 mass ratio. For 1-liter cell culture, ~2 mg of plasmids was pre-mixed with 6 mg of polyethyleneimine (PEI, Polysciences, 23966-100) in 40 mL of fresh medium at room temperature for 30 minutes before transfection. After transfection, the cells were cultured for 48 hours at 37°C and harvested by centrifugation at 4,000 g for 10 min.

For the purification of IPC synthase complex, the harvested cells were resuspended in lysis buffer: 25 mM HEPES pH 7.5, 150 mM NaCl and 1% protease-inhibitor cocktail (Roche), and lysed by sonication on ice. The membrane was solubilized by the addition of 1% (w/v) lauryl maltose neopentyl glycol (LMNG, Anatrace) and 0.1% cholesteryl hemisuccinate Tris salt (CHS, Anatrace) at 4°C for 2 hours. After centrifugation at 20,000 g for 1 hour, the supernatant was collected and loaded into pre-equilibrated anti-Flag M2 affinity resin (Sigma). The resin was washed with washing buffer containing 25 mM HEPES pH 7.5, 150 mM NaCl, 0.01% LMNG and 0.001% CHS, and eluted with washing buffer supplemented with 250 μg/ml 3 × FLAG peptide.

To obtain the nanobody-bound IPC synthase, the purified ALFA-tagged IPC synthase was mixed with purified nanobody at a 1:1.2 molar ratio on ice for 1 hour. The resulting complex was further purified by gel filtration chromatography (Superose 6 10/300 GL, GE Healthcare) with buffer containing 25 mM HEPES pH 7.5, 150 mM NaCl, 0.01% LMNG and 0.001% CHS. The preparation of the ceramide-bound IPC synthase sample follows the procedure described above, with ceramide (APExBIO) at a final concentration of 10 µM added during membrane solubilization and in all subsequent purification buffers.

Cryo-EM data acquisition
For single-particle cryo-EM analysis, a 3 µl aliquot of the ceramide-bound IPC synthase (ALFA-tagged with bound nanobody) at a concentration of 5mg/ml was applied to glow-discharged Quantifoil carbon grids (R1.2/1.3 Au, 300 mesh). The grids were blotted for 4 s at 100% humidity and vitrified in liquid ethane using a FEI Vitrobot Mark IV. For the AbA-bound IPC synthase sample, IPC synthase (ALFA-tagged with bound nanobody) was incubated with 50µM AbA (Med Chem Express, Cat No: HY-P1975) on ice for 1 to 3 hours before freezing the cryo-EM grids.

Cryo-EM data were acquired on a Titan Krios electron microscope (Thermo Fisher) operated at 300 kV, equipped with a Gatan K3 Summit direct electron detector and a GIF Quantum energy filter. Automated data collection was performed using EPU software (Thermo Fisher). Micrographs were recorded under super-resolution counting mode with a physical pixel size of 0.74 Å or 0.926 Å. Defocus values ranged from -1.1 μm to -2.8 μm, with a total accumulated dose of 50 electrons per Å2.

Image processing and 3D reconstruction
The dose-fractionated movies were subjected to motion correction and dose weighting using MotionCor2 51. All subsequent image processing steps were performed using cryoSPARC (v4.7.0)52.

For the IPC synthase-ceramide dataset, 8,250 drift-corrected micrographs were imported into cryoSPARC for patch CTF estimation and template picking. A total of 7,447,058 particles were extracted 4 × binning and subjected to multiple rounds of 2D classification. Ab initio maps were generated and used as initial references for heterogeneous refinement. A cleaned subset of 1,006,952 particles were selected and re-extracted without binning. These particles were further subjected to iterative rounds of ab initio reconstruction and heterogeneous refinement. A final subset of 162,123 particles was selected for non-uniform refinement, resulting a map with an overall resolution of 3.5 Å. A detailed flowchart of the data process is presented in Supplementary Fig. 3. The overall resolution estimates were based on the gold standard Fourier shell correlation (FSC) 0.143 criterion calculations53. The local resolution distribution was estimated using cryoSPARC.

For AbA-incubated IPC synthase sample, we collected two datasets after one-hour and three-hour incubation periods, respectively. Processed analogously to the ceramide-incubated dataset, it was found that the three-hour incubation yielded a structure with higher AbA occupancy. For this long incubation dataset, a total of 10,346 movie stacks were processed and the final reconstruction map with an overall resolution of 3.5 Å from 228,212 particles was obtained. A detailed flowchart of the data processing is presented in Supplementary Fig. 11.

Model building and refinement
The atomic model of ceramide-bound IPC synthase complex was first built. An initial model was generated using AlphaFold3 and rigid-body fitted into the cryo-EM map using Chimera54,55. It was further improved by manual rebuilding in Coot56, guided by the well-defined densities for transmembrane helices and distinctive side-chain features for bulky residues such as Phe, Tyr, Trp, and Arg. Iterative real-space refinement was conducted in PHENIX, with secondary structure and geometry restraints applied57. The resulting model served as the template for building the AbA-bound IPC synthase structure, following a similar procedure. The final models were assessed using MOLPROBITY58. Chimera, ChimeraX59 and PyMOL (Schrödinger, LLC.) were used to prepare the illustrated figures. Statistics of the 3D reconstructions and model refinements were provided in Supplementary Table 1.

Construction of conditional AUR1 or KEI1 knockdown strains
To circumvent the lethality associated with AUR1 deletion, we constructed a conditional AUR1 knockdown strain (YPH499-HIS-GAL-AUR1) by placing AUR1 expression under the control of the tightly regulated GAL1 promoter, which is repressed in glucose-containing medium30. A HIS3-selectable GAL1 promoter replacement cassette (HIS-GAL1) was assembled and introduced into the YPH499 strain via homologous recombination to replace the endogenous AUR1 promoter30,60. Transformants were selected on SGal-His medium (synthetic dropout medium lacking histidine, supplemented with 5% galactose). Correct integration of the HIS-GAL1 cassette was verified by genomic PCR and DNA sequencing, yielding the conditional knockdown YPH499-HIS-GAL-AUR1 strain.

To construct the conditional KEI1 knockdown strain (YPH499-HIS-GAL-KEI1), the endogenous KEI1 promoter was similarly replaced with the HIS-GAL1 cassette using the same strategy. Transformants were selected on SGal-His medium and verified by genomic PCR and DNA sequencing.

Spot assay for growth phenotypic analysis of AUR1 and KEI1 variants
To assess the functional contribution of AUR1 to IPC synthase, the conditional AUR1 knockdown strain (YPH499-HIS-GAL-AUR1) was transformed with either the empty vector pRS424, pRS424 carrying wild-type AUR1, or pRS424 carrying AUR1 variants. The parental YPH499 strain transformed with empty pRS424 was used as the control. Transformants were selected on SLGal-Leu (synthetic dropout medium lacking leucine and containing 5% galactose). Spot assays were performed by first cultivating the cells in liquid SGal-Leu at 30°C with shaking (180 r.p.m.) until reaching exponential phase (OD600 = 0.5). Four 10-fold serial dilutions were prepared, and 5 μL of each dilution was spotted on SGal-Leu or SGlu-Leu (containing 5% glucose instead of galactose). Plates were incubated at 30 °C for 72 hours, and photographed with the 5200CE Image System (TANON). Each assay was performed in triplicate with similar results.

To investigate the role of KEI1, the same assay was carried out using the conditional KEI1 knockdown strain (YPH499-HIS-GAL-KEI1), transformed with either empty pRS424, pRS424 carrying wild-type KEI1, or the parental YPH499 with pRS424 as control. The procedure for growth assays was identical to that described above, and each experiment was independently repeated three times with similar results.

Activity assay via thin-layer chromatography
AUR1 or KEI1 point mutations were introduced by site-directed mutagenesis and confirmed by sequencing. Wild-type and mutated IPC synthases with indicated Aur1 or Kei1 mutations were expressed and purified as described above. The IPC synthase activity was assessed by monitoring fluorescent product formation via incorporation of inositol phosphate from phosphatidylinositol (PI) into NBD-labeled ceramide31. 20µM phosphatidylinositol PI (MCE) or phosphatidylcholine PC (MCE) or phosphatidylethanolamine PE (MCE) was added to 200µl reaction mixture in total containing 25 mM HEPES pH 7.5, 150 mM NaCl and 40µM C6-NBD-ceramide (MCE). The reaction was initiated by adding 2 µg of purified IPCS synthase variants. The reaction was carried out at 30˚C for 30min or 120min. Reactions were terminated by adding 600 μl of chloroform: methanol (2:1, v/v) mixture. Following centrifugation at 1,300g for 2 min, the organic phase was collected and dried under high-purity nitrogen. The reaction products were analyzed by thin-layer chromatography (TLC silica gel 60 F254, Merck) in developing solvent containing chloroform: acetone: acetic acid: methanol: H2O (at volume ratio of 50:20:10:10:5). Fluorescent bands were visualized using a Champ Chemi 610 imaging system (Sinsage).

Immunoprecipitation and immunoblotting
For Aur1 and Kei1 interaction studies, AUR1 and KEI1 genes were subcloned into the pCAG vectors, with a C-terminal FLAG tag fused to AUR1 and an N-terminal Strep tag fused to KEI1. Mutations were introduced via site-directed mutagenesis and confirmed by DNA sequencing. HEK293T cells were cultured and co-transfected with 10 µg of expression plasmids per 10-cm dish using PEI (Polysciences, 23966-100), following the manufacturer’s instructions. For co-transfection, wild-type or mutant AUR1 and KEI1 plasmids were added at a 1:1 mass ratio. After transfection, the cells were cultured at 37 °C for 48 h, harvested and washed with TBST buffer (Tris Buffered Saline with Tween-20).

The harvested cells were resuspended in lysis buffer: 1% (w/v) lauryl maltose neopentyl glycol (LMNG, Anatrace), 0.1% cholesteryl hemisuccinate Tris salt (CHS, Anatrace), 25 mM HEPES pH 7.5, 150 mM NaCl and 1% protease-inhibitor cocktail (Roche), lysed by sonication on ice and centrifuged at 20,000 g for 30 minutes at 4 °C. Immunoprecipitations were performed by subjecting supernatants to either anti-Flag M2 affinity resin (Sigma) or Strep-Tactin resin (IBA), with bound beads washed three times with lysis buffer. Samples were resuspended in SDS-loading buffer and analyzed by 15% SDS-PAGE. Proteins were transferred to PVDF membranes and immunoblotted with the indicated antibodies. Membranes were imaged using the 5200CSE Imaging System (TANON). Sources and dilutions for primary antibodies were as follows: anti-Flag antibody for Flag-tagged Aur1 (Proteintech, 66008-4-lg, 1:5000); anti-Strep antibody for Strep-tagged Kei1 (Solarbio, K114183P, 1:5000). The secondary antibodies used were anti-mouse IgG (Proteintech, SA00001-1, 1:10000). All antibodies were diluted in 3% (w/v) BSA in TBST.

Lipidomics analysis
Lipids were extracted from the protein solution using 750 µL of a chloroform:methanol:Milli-Q water mixture (3:6:1, v/v/v). The mixture was homogenized and centrifuged at 231 g for 1 h at 4 °C. After centrifugation, 350 µL of deionized water and 250 µL of chloroform were added to induce phase separation. The sample was centrifuged again, and the lower organic phase containing lipids was collected into a clean tube. To maximize lipid recovery, 450 µL of chloroform was added to the remaining aqueous phase, and lipid extraction was repeated once. The combined organic phases were dried using a SpeedVac under OH mode, and the resulting lipid extracts were stored at −80 °C for further analysis. The upper aqueous phase and the residual protein pellet were dried in a SpeedVac under H2O mode. The dried protein pellet was subsequently used for total protein quantification. Lipidomic analysis was performed using a Shimadzu Nexera 20AD-HPLC/ExionLC-AD system coupled to a Sciex QTRAP 6500 PLUS mass spectrometer. Polar lipid classes were separated by normal phase (NP) HPLC using a TUP-HB silica column (150 × 2.1 mm, 3 µm). The mobile phases consisted of (A) chloroform:methanol:ammonium hydroxide (89.5:10:0.5, v/v/v) and (B) chloroform:methanol:ammonium hydroxide:water (55:39:0.5:5.5, v/v/v/v). Multiple reaction monitoring (MRM) transitions were optimized for the comparative quantification of various polar lipid species. Quantification of individual lipid species was performed relative to spiked internal standards, including d9-PC32:0(16:0/16:0), d9-PC36:1p(18:0p/18:1), d7-PE33:1(15:0/18:1), d9-PE36:1p(18:0p/18:1), d31-PS(d31-16:0/18:1), d7-PA33:1(15:0/18:1), d7-PG33:1(15:0/18:1), d7-PI33:1(15:0/18:1), C17-SL, d5-CL72:8(18:2)₄, Cer d18:1/15:0-d7, C12:0 Cer-1-P, d9-SM d18:1/18:1, C8-GluCer, C8-GalCer, d3-LacCer d18:1/16:0, Gb3 d18:1/17:0, Pd7-LPC18:1, d7-LPE18:1, C17-LPI, C17-LPA, C17-LPS, C17-LPG, d17:1 Sph, and d17:1 S1P (all from Avanti Polar Lipids). GM3-d18:1/18:0-d3 was obtained from Matreya LLC. Free fatty acids were quantified using d31-16:0 (Sigma-Aldrich) and d8-L20:4 (Cayman Chemical) as internal standards. Free cholesterol and cholesteryl esters were analyzed in atmospheric pressure chemical ionization (APCI) mode using a Jasper HPLC system coupled to a Sciex 4500 MD mass spectrometer, as previously described. Quantification was performed with d6-cholesterol and d6-C18:0 cholesteryl ester (CE) (CDN Isotopes) as internal standards.

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

The manuscript by Hingjun Yu and colleagues describes the cryo-EM structure of the fungal inositol phosphorylceramide (IPC) synthase from S. cerevisiae, the enzyme responsible for inositol phosphorylceramide synthesis. IPC is a key component of fungal membranes, and is absent from mammalian cells. It is therefore an important anti-fungal drug target. The authors find that IPC synthase is a heterodimer of the Aur1 and Kei1 subunits. The dimer interface is stabilised by a phospholipid and two lipid alkyl chains. The authors identify H255, H294 and D98 of the Aur1 subunit as being essential for catalysis and suggest that these three residues form a catalytic triad. A HHD triad is also found in other fungal IPC synthases despite low sequence similarity. The authors determined a structure of the complex with the antifungal agent aureobasidin (AbA) and suggest AbA acts as a competitive inhibitor to block ceramide binding. Finally, the authors test models of the Aur1-Kei dimer interface, phospholipid binding and catalysis using mutagenesis.

In general this is an interesting paper. The figures are clear and the cryo-EM work is sound. Use of the ALFA-binding nanobody to increase size and help alignment was innovative.

1. When describing the structure, the authors do not compare and contrast with other membrane protein structures. A brief comment on the relatedness of IPC synthase to other membrane protein structures would be informative and useful, or is this a novel structure?
2. The identification of a phospholipid and two alkyl chains at the Aur1-Kei subunit interface is of interest. However, the two lone alkyl chains are a little unusual. Are these attached to a phospholipid whose head group is disordered?
3. The authors suggest that the catalytic triad of His255, His294 and Asp298 catalyse inositol phosphate transfer. A reaction schematic to show the catalytic reaction mechanism would be helpful.
4. Where is the binding site for phosphatidylinositol in Aur1? How is IPC synthase specific for phosphatidylinositol and not able use phosphatidylcholine (PC) or phosphatidylethanolamine?
5. The authors suggest that in the presence of AbA, the aromatic side chain of Phe 158 rotates 90°. It is not entirely obvious that this would be clear at 3.5 A resolution. The authors should show cryo-EM density that supports this conclusion.
6. I didn’t see reference in Supplementary Fig. 2.
7. ‘Comparation’ is not an English word

### Reviewer 2

This study presents cryo-EM structures of IPC synthase in complex with its substrate ceramide and the inhibitor AbA. The authors successfully identified the substrate-binding cavity and the AbA inhibitor pocket, providing critical insights into the enzyme’s catalytic mechanism. Complementary biochemical and cell-based assays robustly validate the essential role of IPC synthase catalytic activity in fungal sphingolipid biosynthesis. Notably, the resolution of a high-resolution structure for this ~71 kDa membrane protein—achieved through the combination of an ALFA epitope tag and a high-affinity nanobody—represents a significant methodological advancement in the field of membrane protein structural biology.

Overall, the topic is of interest given the essential role of IPC synthase in fungal sphingolipid metabolism and its potential as an antifungal drug target. However, I note that a closely related study by Wu et al. (Nature Communications, 2025) has already reported high-resolution structures of the Aur1–Kei1 complex bound to AbA, identifying the catalytic H–H–D triad, key resistance mutations, and the dimeric architecture. Therefore, my comments will focus more on the novelty part of this work relative to Wu’s paper.

Major points:
1. A major concern with the current manuscript is the insufficient acknowledgment of critical related literature. Wu et al. reported cryo-EM structures of the S. cerevisiae Aur1–Kei1 complex bound to Aureobasidin A, describing the same protein target and inhibitor, and this work should be explicitly cited in both the Introduction and Discussion. The authors need to carefully compare their findings with those of Wu et al. to highlight both consistencies (such as the catalytic H–H–D triad, AbA resistance mutations, and overall architecture) and differences (including the ceramide-bound state and lipid-mediated assembly) to avoid overstating novelty. In addition, because IPC synthase belongs to the sphingomyelin synthase (SMS) family, readers would benefit from a broader discussion that integrates previous structural and biochemical studies on SMS enzymes. Such a comparison could illuminate how the H–H–D catalytic triad and substrate positioning in IPC synthase relate to SMS enzymes, and whether conserved or divergent features explain differences in substrate specificity. Incorporating these key references and analyses will provide proper context, clarify the unique contributions of the present study, and strengthen its impact.
2. The capture of ceramide in the active site is indeed a valuable addition not present in Wu et al., and the authors support their proposed structural model and catalytic mechanism with mutagenesis of key residues in the reaction chamber, which resulted in reduced activity. However, to strengthen this conclusion, they should provide evidence that the observed effects are not due to global misfolding of the enzyme but rather specific to the catalytic center—for example, by assessing the stability or expression of the purified mutant proteins with size-exclusion FPLC. Moreover, the H157A mutant retains ~50% activity, showing the least impairment among the catalytic site variants; a brief discussion of why different mutations within the catalytic center yield varied activity reductions would be helpful. Finally, it remains uncertain whether the ceramide density reflects a true catalytic intermediate or a trapped state introduced during purification and exposure to detergents or exogenous lipids. The authors should discuss the likelihood of ceramide incorporation under their preparation conditions and address how well this state represents in vivo substrate binding.
3. Another point that warrants attention is the interpretation of the lipid-mediated heterodimer stabilization of the Aur1–Kei1 complex. The identification of a phospholipid density bridging the interface is intriguing. However, several concerns remain. First, the exact identity of the lipid is not determined, and it is unclear whether this represents a physiologically specific cofactor, a detergent-derived molecule, or a general phospholipid from the purification system. The authors should clarify the lipid assignment and, if possible, provide mass spectrometry or biochemical analysis to strengthen this claim. Second, it is important to discuss whether this lipid-mediated interaction is unique to IPC synthase or could represent a more general feature among the sphingomyelin synthase family. Finally, the authors should place their findings in context with prior work: Gong et al. noted lipid-like densities at the interface but did not ascribe functional significance, so a more explicit comparison would help delineate what is novel here. Overall, while the lipid-mediated stabilization model is a potentially important advance, its physiological specificity and mechanistic implications require more careful discussion and validation.
4. In the AbA-bound IPC synthase complex (Fig. 4), the reported unassigned density within the catalytic cavity does not convincingly fit the 3D structure of the AbA inhibitor. This discrepancy raises critical concerns regarding the interpretation of the AbA-bound state. Specifically: (1) does the IPCS–ALFA construct reduce AbA binding affinity compared to the wild-type enzyme, and (2) could AbA be hydrolyzed within the catalytic cavity, thereby explaining the incomplete density? If either hypothesis is plausible, the authors should provide biochemical validation: for example, quantifying AbA binding affinity (e.g., Kd) for IPCS–ALFA versus wild-type using SPR or ITC, or testing for AbA hydrolysis by LC–MS to detect cleavage products. If neither explanation holds, the authors must rigorously demonstrate that the unassigned density corresponds to bound AbA rather than endogenous lipids co-purified with the protein. The current assertion that AbA binding is “dynamic” is not sufficiently supported. Rigorous validation of this density is essential to substantiate the proposed inhibition mechanism.

Some minor points:
Fig. 2B (SDS-PAGE) and Figs. 2I-J (Co-IP):
In the SDS-PAGE results of Fig. 2B (lane for purified Aur1), what do the high-molecular-weight bands above the Aur1 band represent? Similar bands are observed in the co-immunoprecipitation assays (Figs. 2I-J). Do they correspond to glycosylated forms of Aur1? If so, glycan density should be detectable in your cryo-EM maps, why is this density absent in the manuscript? What is the biological significance of Aur1 glycosylation?
Line 246: While the Ser residue in the canonical Ser–His–Asp catalytic triad typically provides the nucleophilic hydroxyl oxygen essential for catalysis, the specific role of S253 (located in EL3) in Aur1 during sphingolipid synthesis remains unclear. Notably, mutagenesis of S253 does not completely abolish enzymatic activity, raising questions about whether it truly functions as the nucleophile in the reaction. To clarify this discrepancy, the authors could strengthen their study by (i) providing a comparative analysis of S253’s position and function relative to the catalytic Ser residues in classical triads, and (ii) performing additional mutagenesis, such as S253C or S253T substitutions, to quantify enzymatic activity and evaluate whether side-chain chemistry influences catalysis. Such data would help resolve whether S253 is directly catalytic or plays an auxiliary structural/positioning role in Aur1’s mechanism.

### Reviewer 3

I co-reviewed this manuscript with one of the reviewers who provided the listed reports. This is part of the Nature Communications initiative to facilitate training in peer review and to provide appropriate recognition for Early Career Researchers who co-review manuscripts.

Point-to-point responses to the reviewers’ comments

REVIEWER COMMENTS
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
The manuscript by Hingjun Yu and colleagues describes the cryo-EM structure of the
fungal inositol phosphorylceramide (IPC) synthase from S. cerevisiae, the enzyme
responsible for inositol phosphorylceramide synthesis. IPC is a key component of
fungal membranes, and is absent from mammalian cells. It is therefore an important
anti-fungal drug target. The authors find that IPC synthase is a heterodimer of the Aur1
and Kei1 subunits. The dimer interface is stabilised by a phospholipid and two lipid
alkyl chains. The authors identify H255, H294 and D98 of the Aur1 subunit as being
essential for catalysis and suggest that these three residues form a catalytic triad. A
HHD triad is also found in other fungal IPC synthases despite low sequence similarity.
The authors determined a structure of the complex with the antifungal agent
aureobasidin (AbA) and suggest AbA acts as a competitive inhibitor to block ceramide
binding. Finally, the authors test models of the Aur1-Kei dimer interface, phospholipid
binding and catalysis using mutagenesis.
In general this is an interesting paper. The figures are clear and the cryo-EM work is
sound. Use of the ALFA-binding nanobody to increase size and help alignment was
innovative.
Response: We thank the reviewer for the support and the valuable comments. They are
so helpful to improve our manuscript. We have revised our manuscript accordingly.
1. When describing the structure, the authors do not compare and contrast with other
membrane protein structures. A brief comment on the relatedness of IPC synthase to
other membrane protein structures would be informative and useful, or is this a novel
structure?
Response: We thank the reviewer for this insightful suggestion. In response, we have
added a section comparing the IPC synthase structure with other known membrane
proteins identified by DALI analysis [1]. This analysis not only underscores the
structural novelty of both Aur1 and Kei1 but also reveals a conserved LPT (lipid
phosphatase/phosphotransferase) fold within the catalytic subunit Aur1. The related
description has been incorporated into the revised manuscript (Lines 190-219 on Page
7-8; Supplementary Fig. 5) as follows:
“A DALI server search for the regulatory subunit Kei1 of the IPC heterodimer did not
yield any structurally similar homologs [1]. In contrast, for the catalytic subunit Aur1,
although the overall architecture of Aur1 differs from previously reported structures, a
DALI homology search identified several membrane-protein structures that resemble a
portion of Aur1’s transmembrane topology (residues 143-314) (Supplementary Fig.
5). These include (in a descending order of Z-score): Lipid A 1-Phosphatase (LpxE),
Glucose-6-phosphatase (G6PC1), Phosphatidylglycerophosphatase B (PgpB), and
Sphingomyelin synthase-related protein 1 (SMSr) [2-5]. Despite their low sequence
conservation (<10% identities), structural superposition revealed that a cluster of five
successive transmembrane helices of these proteins adopt comparable topologies,
whereas the remaining regions diverge in both fold and number of transmembrane
helices (Supplementary Fig. 5). Notably, all these structurally related proteins belong
to lipid phosphatase/phosphotransferase (LPT) family, most members of which are
integral membrane enzymes catalyzing the dephosphorylation or phosphotransfer
reactions of diverse phospho-lipid or phospho-carbohydrate substrate [6]. This suggests
that these enzymes (including Aur1, LpxE, G6PC1, PgpB, SMSr) share a conserved
structural module, which we term the LPT fold. This fold exhibits several common
features (Supplementary Fig. 5): it comprises five transmembrane helices, often
situated in the C-terminal region (except in G6PC1); the luminal loop (e.g., EL4 in Aur1)
connecting the last two helices harbors a catalytically essential histidine residue (e.g.,
H294 in Aur1; see Discussions for further mechanistic details). Despite this conserved
core, notable structural variations exist. The orientation and length of the topologically
equivalent transmembrane helices differ among family members. For instance, the first
helix of the module is continuous in SMSr (TM5) but kinked in Aur1 (TM4), LpxE
(TM1), G6PC1 (TM1), and PgpB (TM2), reflecting structural variability within this
shared scaffold (see Discussion for further comparison).”
Notably, this analysis also provides critical clues for elucidating its catalytic
mechanism, as further discussed in our comparative analysis of the active sites in the
revised manuscript (Lines 509-529 on Page 18-19; Supplementary Fig. 13).

“We propose a two-step catalytic mechanism for IPC synthesis (Fig. 3I). In the first
step, D298 activates H294 to initiate a nucleophilic attack on the phosphate group of
PI, leading to the formation of an enzyme–phosphoinositol intermediate and the release
of diacylglycerol (DAG). In the second step, H255 activates the hydroxyl group of an
incoming ceramide, which attacks the intermediate and transfers the phosphorylinositol
moiety to ceramide, ultimately forming inositol phosphorylceramide (IPC).”

4. Where is the binding site for phosphatidylinositol in Aur1? How is IPC synthase
specific for phosphatidylinositol and not able use phosphatidylcholine (PC) or
phosphatidylethanolamine?
Response: We thank the reviewer for raising these important questions. To address
these points, we performed molecular docking of PI into the Aur1 structure
(Supplementary Fig. 9A). The result indicates that PI occupies the reaction chamber
identified in our ceramide-bound IPCS structure. Specifically, the inositol group of PI
is nestled deep within a pocket formed by transmembrane helices TM5–TM7 and
luminal loops EL3 and EL4 (Supplementary Fig. 9B-C). The shape of this pocket
appears to optimally accommodate the bulkier inositol group of PI (Supplementary
Fig. 9C-D), likely underlying the observed phospholipid preference (Fig. 1C).
Importantly, in this binding pose, the phosphate group of PI is positioned in close
proximity to the catalytically essential residues H255 and H294 (Supplementary Fig.
9D), which is consistent with our proposed reaction mechanism described above (Fig.
3I).
The corresponding descriptions have been incorporated into the revised manuscript
(Lines 334-347, Page 12; Supplementary Fig. 9).

Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
This study presents cryo-EM structures of IPC synthase in complex with its substrate
ceramide and the inhibitor AbA. The authors successfully identified the substrate-
binding cavity and the AbA inhibitor pocket, providing critical insights into the
enzyme’s catalytic mechanism. Complementary biochemical and cell-based assays
robustly validate the essential role of IPC synthase catalytic activity in fungal
sphingolipid biosynthesis. Notably, the resolution of a high-resolution structure for this
~71 kDa membrane protein—achieved through the combination of an ALFA epitope tag
and a high-affinity nanobody—represents a significant methodological advancement in
the field of membrane protein structural biology.
Overall, the topic is of interest given the essential role of IPC synthase in fungal
sphingolipid metabolism and its potential as an antifungal drug target. However, I note
that a closely related study by Wu et al. (Nature Communications, 2025) has already
reported high-resolution structures of the Aur1–Kei1 complex bound to AbA, identifying
the catalytic H–H–D triad, key resistance mutations, and the dimeric architecture.
Therefore, my comments will focus more on the novelty part of this work relative to
Wu’s paper.
Response: We thank the reviewer for the support and the important comments to
improve the manuscript. We have revised our manuscript accordingly.
Major points:
1. A major concern with the current manuscript is the insufficient acknowledgment of
critical related literature. Wu et al. reported cryo-EM structures of the S. cerevisiae
Aur1–Kei1 complex bound to Aureobasidin A, describing the same protein target and
inhibitor, and this work should be explicitly cited in both the Introduction and
Discussion. The authors need to carefully compare their findings with those of Wu et al.
to highlight both consistencies (such as the catalytic H–H–D triad, AbA resistance
mutations, and overall architecture) and differences (including the ceramide-bound
state and lipid-mediated assembly) to avoid overstating novelty.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this important comment. We fully agree that the
study by Wu et al. should be appropriately acknowledged and compared. As
recommended, we have revised the manuscript to explicitly compare our study with
this recently published work and to clarify our unique contributions (see Lines 530-563
on Page 19-20) as mentioned below:
During the preparation of this manuscript, Wu et al. reported the cryo-EM structure
of the S. cerevisiae Aur1–Kei1 IPC synthase complex (IPCS) bound to Aureobasidin A
(AbA) [1]. To overcome challenges posed by the small size of IPCS (~71 kd) and the
absence of prominent soluble domain for particle alignment, these two studies used
distinct strategies. Wu et al. achieved structure determination by imposing C2
symmetry on a dimerized complex, but beyond the AbA-bound form, they were unable
to resolve additional functional states due to the lack of AbA-mediated stabilization [1].
In contrast, we employed an independent approach utilizing an ALFA tag and a
nanobody as fiducial markers (Supplementary Fig. 1), which enabled us to capture
multiple functional states of IPCS, including both the AbA- and ceramide-bound forms
(Fig. 3, Fig. 4).
Despite being determined independently, the structural insights from AbA-bound
states from both studies are in excellent agreement, uncovering consistent overall
architecture, drug-binding site, and mechanisms of drug inhibition and resistance.
Notably, our structural and functional analyses revealed a stabilizing role of lipids at
the Aur1-Kei1 interface (Fig. 2F-J), a feature implicated but not explored in another
study [1].
Beyond these consensus findings, our work provides several unique insights. While
analysis of catalytic mechanism was almost not included in their study, Wu et al.
proposed that Aur1 and SMSr share similar substrate-binding pockets and catalytic
mechanism based on analogy with the substrate-bound SMSr structure [1]. In contrast,
our ceramide-bound Aur1 structure—exclusively obtained in this study—reveals an
adapted reaction chamber and ceramide-binding mode (Supplementary Fig. 12).
Moreover, this divergence also extends to the catalytic mechanism (Supplementary
Fig. 13): while SMSr relies on additional catalytic residues (E205 and D295) absent in
Aur1 and canonical LPT members [2-3], our data supports an alternative mechanism
consistent with that of canonical LPT enzymes (see discussions below for more detailed
comparison between Aur1 and SMSr).
Importantly, by comparing our AbA-bound and ceramide-bound states, we directly
visualize the competitive relationship between substrate and drug (Fig. 4E). This
comparison analysis further captures the conformational dynamics within Aur1,
revealing how AbA binding induces pronounced rearrangements in key drug-
interacting residues and the adjacent TM2–TM3 region (Fig. 4E-F). The exclusive
comparison of multiple functional states advances the molecular insights into AbA
binding and AbA-mediated inhibition.

[1] Wu, X., Gong, X. & Xie, T. Mechanisms of aureobasidin A inhibition and drug
resistance in a fungal IPC synthase complex. Nature Communications 16, 5010 (2025).
[2] Hu, K. et al. Cryo-EM structure of human sphingomyelin synthase and its
mechanistic implications for sphingomyelin synthesis. Nat Struct Mol Biol 31, 884-895
(2024).
[3] Sigal, Y. J., McDermott, M. I. & Morris, A. J. Integral membrane lipid
phosphatases/phosphotransferases: common structure and diverse functions. Biochem
J 387, 281-293 (2005).
In addition, because IPC synthase belongs to the sphingomyelin synthase (SMS) family,
readers would benefit from a broader discussion that integrates previous structural and
biochemical studies on SMS enzymes. Such a comparison could illuminate how the H–
H–D catalytic triad and substrate positioning in IPC synthase relate to SMS enzymes,
and whether conserved or divergent features explain differences in substrate specificity.
Incorporating these key references and analyses will provide proper context, clarify the
unique contributions of the present study, and strengthen its impact.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this insightful suggestion. Following this
comment and a related point from Reviewer 1 (Point #1), we have now incorporated a
thorough comparison between IPC synthase and structural homologs (with low
sequence homologies) identified through DALI analysis [1], including the human
sphingomyelin synthase (SMS) family member-SMSr [2]. This analysis not only
highlights the structural novelty of Aur1 and Kei1 but also identifies a conserved LPT
(lipid phosphatase/phosphotransferase) fold within the catalytic subunit Aur1, offering
key mechanistic clues for understanding its catalytic mechanism (see also our response
to Reviewer 1, Point #1).
Furthermore, in direct response to this suggestion, we have conducted a detailed
comparative analysis between IPCS Aur1 and SMSr [2]. These results help delineate
their conserved and notable divergent features (as described in the revised manuscript
on Lines 488-529, Pages 17–19), as listed below:
(1) Structural comparison between IPCS Aur1 and SMSr:
Despite their limited sequence identity (<10%) between IPCS Aur1 and SMSr,
their
structures can be superimposed with an RMSD of 3.5 Å over 264 aligned residues
(Supplementary Fig. 12A-B). Beyond the conserved LPT fold (Supplementary Fig.
5), TM1 of SMSr can also align with TM3 of Aur1, though the latter become
discontinuous in Aur1. Despite their overall resemblance, key differences emerge near
the reaction chamber (Supplementary Fig. 12C-E). First, in Aur1, TM4—which lines
the side wall of the reaction chamber and corresponds to the continuous TM2 in
SMSr—is interrupted and kinked by a unique ‘Gly-Ala-Pro’ loop. Second, the extended
luminal EL3 loop of Aur1, which caps the reaction chamber, adopts a markedly
different conformation from the corresponding EL2 of SMSr. Consistent with these
structural variations, although ceramide occupies comparable positions within the
reaction chambers, its binding pose differs between the two enzymes. Given their
distinct substrate specificities (PI for Aur1 versus PE for SMSr), it is conceivable that
the structural differences surrounding the reaction chamber may underlie this
divergence, a hypothesis that merits further investigation.
(2) Comparison of the catalytic mechanisms between IPCS Aur1 and SMSr
Consistent with the shared LPT module (Supplementary Fig. 5), detailed structural
comparisons of Aur1 with other LPT members further reveal that the H-H-D catalytic
triad (comprising one histidine from the C2 motif and a histidine-aspartate pair from
the ‘HXXXD’ C3 motif) is conserved and arranged in a remarkably similar spatial
configuration [3] (Supplementary Fig. 13). In particular, the catalytic histidine within
the C3 motif (e.g., H294 in Aur1) is absolutely conserved, suggesting a unified catalytic
mechanism. In our proposed catalytic model for Aur1 (Fig. 3I), the invariant C3
histidine (H294), activated by D298 in the same motif, acts as a nucleophile to form a
transient phosphohistidine intermediate, while the C2 histidine (H255) facilitates
further phosphate transfer. This mechanism is consistent with those established for LPT
enzymes such as LpxE, G6PC1, and PgpB, among others [3-6]. In contrast, SMSr has
been proposed to employ a distinct catalytic strategy, wherein two catalytic residues
(first, C2 histidine H301, activated by E205; second, D295, activated by C3 H344 and
D348) mediates two sequential catalytic steps [2]. It is noted that these additional
catalytic residues in SMSr (E205 and D295) are outside the C2 and C3 motifs and are
not conserved in Aur1 and several LPT members such as LpxE, G6PC1 and PgpB
(Supplementary Fig. 13B-F). These functional distinctions suggest that divergent
catalytic mechanism may occur in the context of conserved H-H-D catalytic triad,
warranting further investigation.

2. The capture of ceramide in the active site is indeed a valuable addition not present
in Wu et al., and the authors support their proposed structural model and catalytic
mechanism with mutagenesis of key residues in the reaction chamber, which resulted in
reduced activity. However, to strengthen this conclusion, they should provide evidence
that the observed effects are not due to global misfolding of the enzyme but rather
specific to the catalytic center—for example, by assessing the stability or expression of
the purified mutant proteins with size-exclusion FPLC.
Moreover, the H157A mutant retains ~50% activity, showing the least impairment
among the catalytic site variants; a brief discussion of why different mutations within
the catalytic center yield varied activity reductions would be helpful.
Finally, it remains uncertain whether the ceramide density reflects a true catalytic
intermediate or a trapped state introduced during purification and exposure to
detergents or exogenous lipids. The authors should discuss the likelihood of ceramide
incorporation under their preparation conditions and address how well this state
represents in vivo substrate binding.
Response: We thank the review for these insightful comments, which have been
addressed accordingly in our revised manuscript.
Regarding the concern about potential misfolding of the mutants, we first verified
that all key mutants were expressed at levels comparable to the wild-type (WT) enzyme,
as shown by western blot analysis (Supplementary Fig. 2C). Furthermore, in direct
response to the reviewer's suggestion, we purified these mutants and assessed their
states by size-exclusion FPLC (Superose 6 Increase 10/300 GL column). The elution
profiles of all mutants were similar to that of the WT complex (Supplementary Fig.
2D), which is consistent with their maintained subunit stoichiometry (Supplementary
Fig. 2B). Together, these data support the proper folding of all mutants analyzed. We
have incorporated these results and corresponding discussion into the revised
manuscript (Lines 312-315, Page 11).
About the varied activity impairment of different catalytic site mutants, it shows a
hierarchy of functional contributions that offers valuable insights into the catalytic
mechanism. Mutations H255A, H294A, and D298A each completely abolished IPC
synthase activity (Fig. 3G-H), supporting them as essential members of the catalytic
triad. In contrast, other active-site mutations (H293A, H157A, and S253A) led to
varying degrees of partial activity loss, with H157A, located farthest from the catalytic
triad, showing the least impairment (~50% residual activity) (Fig. 3G-H). This
gradation in mutational effects suggests that while the catalytic triad (H255, H294,
D298) is indispensable for the core enzymatic reaction, neighboring residues such as
H157, S253, and H293 also contribute to activity. These latter auxiliary residues may
help maintain optimal catalytic geometry, fine-tune substrate orientation, or stabilize
the active-site environment, though their precise mechanistic roles await further
elucidation. We have included a discussion of this interpretation in the revised
manuscript (Lines 315-333, Page 11-12).
About ceramide, following reviewer’s suggestion, we have considered it carefully
and would like to present the following evidence supporting its incorporation and
functional relevance. As detailed in the Methods section (Lines 615-622, Page 22),
ceramide was the only exogenous lipid added throughout the purification procedure for
preparing the ceramide-bound complex. While LMNG (lauryl maltose neopentyl glycol)
and CHS (cholesteryl hemisuccinate) were employed as two essential purification
detergents, the well-defined electron density closely matches the ceramide structure and
cannot be reasonably fitted to either detergent (Supplementary Fig. 4B and 4D):
neither to CHS with a distinct sterol scaffold, nor to LMNG with bulky maltose-based
headgroup that is also sterically incompatible with the narrow, groove-shaped active
site. Importantly, the ceramide headgroup is positioned in proximity to the catalytic
triad, consistent with the proposed reaction mechanism of IPC synthase and canonical
LPT enzymes [1] (Fig. 3D and 3I). Moreover, the bound ceramide conformation
sterically clashes with AbA, suggesting a competitive inhibition mechanism for this
drug (Fig. 4E). Together, these evidences strongly support ceramide incorporation as
well as the functional relevance of the observed ceramide-bound state. We have
included a discussion of this interpretation in the revised manuscript (Lines 287-295,

3. Another point that warrants attention is the interpretation of the lipid-mediated
heterodimer stabilization of the Aur1–Kei1 complex. The identification of a
phospholipid density bridging the interface is intriguing. However, several concerns
remain. First, the exact identity of the lipid is not determined, and it is unclear whether
this represents a physiologically specific cofactor, a detergent-derived molecule, or a
general phospholipid from the purification system. The authors should clarify the
lipid assignment and, if possible, provide mass spectrometry or biochemical analysis to
strengthen this claim.
Second, it is important to discuss whether this lipid-mediated interaction is unique
to IPC synthase or could represent a more general feature among the sphingomyelin
synthase family.
Finally, the authors should place their findings in context with prior work:
Gong et al. noted lipid-like densities at the interface but did not ascribe functional
significance, so a more explicit comparison would help delineate what is novel here.
Overall, while the lipid-mediated stabilization model is a potentially important advance,
its physiological specificity and mechanistic implications require more careful
discussion and validation.
Response: We thank the review for these insightful suggestions. We have revised
accordingly.
About the assignment of the phospholipid, we have considered it carefully and
would like to present the following consideration. It is important to note that no
exogenous phospholipids were added during the purification of either the ceramide-
bound or AbA-bound complexes. The consistent presence of similar lipid-like densities
in both structural states supports the identification as an endogenous phospholipid.
Furthermore, although LMNG and CHS were used as detergents during purification,
the observed density matches a phospholipid structure and cannot be reasonably fitted
to either CHS (with a distinct sterol scaffold) or LMNG (with bulky maltose-based
headgroup) (Supplementary Fig. 4A, 4D). Moreover, following reviewer’s suggestion,
we also performed lipidomics analysis via mass spectrometry of lipids co-purified with
IPC synthase. The result confirmed the presence of several lipid species, most notably
phospholipid, providing additional support for our lipid assignment (Supplementary
Fig. 4C). We have included a discussion of this interpretation in the revised manuscript
(Lines 255-263, Page 9-10).
As for the uniqueness of this lipid-mediated interaction, the key lipid-interacting
residues in Aur1 (K274 and K314) are highly conserved across IPC synthases from
major fungal pathogens (Supplementary Fig. 7), yet are not conserved in
sphingomyelin synthase family members such as SMSr (Supplementary Fig. 12E).
Furthermore, the lipid-mediated stabilization occurs specifically between the catalytic
Aur1 and regulatory Kei1 subunits. This heteromeric architecture appears to be a
distinctive feature of IPC synthase, as sphingomyelin synthases like SMSr function
without regulatory partners [1] (Supplementary Fig. 5A, 5E). Therefore, this lipid-
mediated inter-subunit interaction appear a general mechanism among fungal IPC
synthases but is absent in the sphingomyelin synthase family. We have included a
discussion of this interpretation in the revised manuscript (Lines 457-463, Page 16).
As for the third suggestion, in response, we have now added an explicit comparison
with the study by Gong et al. in the revised manuscript (Lines 530-563, Pages 19-20;
please see also our response to Reviewer 2, Point #1), including a specific discussion
of these interface lipids (Lines 544-546, Page 19). While Gong et al. briefly mentioned
lipid-like densities at the Aur1–Kei1 interface, they did not assign these densities or
explore their functional relevance [2]. In contrast, our work combines structural and
conservation analysis (Fig. 2F–H) and functional/biochemical assays (Fig. 2I–J;
Supplementary Fig. 4C) to assign these lipid densities and to identify lipid-interacting
residues, highlighting lipid-mediated heterodimer stabilization at the Aur1–Kei1
interface. Notably, our study and Gong et al. employed independent structural
determination strategies (please see more details about this in our response to Reviewer
interfacial lipid density [2]. This consistency reinforces the validity of the lipid-
mediated stabilization mechanism.

4. In the AbA-bound IPC synthase complex (Fig. 4), the reported unassigned density
within the catalytic cavity does not convincingly fit the 3D structure of the AbA inhibitor.
This discrepancy raises critical concerns regarding the interpretation of the AbA-bound
state. Specifically: (1) does the IPCS–ALFA construct reduce AbA binding affinity
compared to the wild-type enzyme, and (2) could AbA be hydrolyzed within the catalytic
cavity, thereby explaining the incomplete density? If either hypothesis is plausible, the
authors should provide biochemical validation: for example, quantifying AbA binding
affinity (e.g., Kd) for IPCS–ALFA versus wild-type using SPR or ITC, or testing for AbA
hydrolysis by LC–MS to detect cleavage products. If neither explanation holds, the
authors must rigorously demonstrate that the unassigned density corresponds to bound
AbA rather than endogenous lipids co-purified with the protein. The current assertion
that AbA binding is “dynamic” is not sufficiently supported. Rigorous validation of this
density is essential to substantiate the proposed inhibition mechanism.
Response: We thank the reviewer for raising this important point. Our biochemical data
showed that the ALFA-tagged IPCS construct maintained catalytic efficiency and AbA
sensitivity comparable to the wild-type enzyme, regardless of whether the Nb was
bound (Fig. 4B). This indicates that neither the tag nor Nb binding impaired enzyme
function or inhibitor binding. In addition, the compound we used consistently exhibited
stable inhibitory activity in our assays and to our knowledge, there appears no previous
studies reporting the hydrolysis of AbA.
To directly address the reviewer’s concern regarding the incomplete density, we
systematically optimized the sample preparation procedure. By extending the AbA
incubation time from 1 to 3 hours, we achieved substantially improved drug occupancy,
which allowed us to determine the complex structure at an overall resolution of 3.5 Å
(Supplementary Fig. 11A–H). The resulting cryo-EM map displayed clear and
continuous density corresponding to the intact AbA molecule (Supplementary
Fig. 11I), indicating that the previously observed partial density likely resulted from a
low-occupancy state of the inhibitor.
This high-occupancy AbA-bound structure reveals detailed interactions of AbA
within the Aur1 reaction chamber, involving multiple residues, and confirms that H157
and F158 (located on the linker between TM4a and TM4b) constitute the key binding
site (Fig. 4D), consistent with our original proposal. These findings further underscore
the functional importance of these two residues (H157 and F158) in the development
of AbA resistance (Fig. 4H), as proposed in our original and current manuscript.
Notably, by comparing this new AbA-bound structure with our ceramide-bound
IPCS structure, we directly demonstrate the competitive relationship between substrate
and inhibitor (Fig. 4E), as well as pronounced conformational rearrangements in key
drug-interacting residues and the adjacent TM2–TM3 region (Fig. 4E-F). These
structural insights substantially advances the molecular insights into AbA binding and
AbA-mediated inhibition..
The related description of this new AbA-bound state has been incorporated into the
revised manuscript (Lines 388-426, Page 14-15).

glycosylation?
Response: We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. In response, we have
performed additional analyses of Aur1 glycosylation, which are now included in the
revised manuscript (Lines 107-114, Page 4; Lines 151-159, Page 6).
SDS–PAGE and western blot analyses of the purified IPCS complex revealed that
Aur1, but not Kei1, displayed several high–molecular–weight species (Supplementary
Fig. 1G-H). Treatment of the purified complex with PNGase F eliminated these higher–
molecular-weight forms of Aur1, confirming that they arise from N-linked
glycosylation (Supplementary Fig. 1G-H). Enzymatic assays further showed that
removal of N-glycans had minimal impact on IPC synthase activity (Supplementary
Fig. 1I). We have included a discussion of this interpretation in the revised manuscript
(Lines 107-114, Page 4).
Notably, although we confirmed the presence of N-glycosylation on Aur1
(Supplementary Fig. 1G-H), the specific glycosylation site could not be
unambiguously assigned. Among the three predicted glycosylation sites (N132, N243,
and N367), N367 is located in a disordered region of the structure. In contrast, while
N132 and N243 lie in ordered regions, neither exhibits clear glycan density. This
suggests that these sites are either unmodified or contain highly flexible glycans, with
the latter consistent with the minimal enzymatic effects observed upon glycan removal
(Supplementary Fig. 1I). We have included a discussion of this interpretation in the
revised manuscript (Lines 151-159, Page 6).

Line 246: While the Ser residue in the canonical Ser–His–Asp catalytic triad typically
provides the nucleophilic hydroxyl oxygen essential for catalysis, the specific role of
S253 (located in EL3) in Aur1 during sphingolipid synthesis remains unclear. Notably,
mutagenesis of S253 does not completely abolish enzymatic activity, raising questions
about whether it truly functions as the nucleophile in the reaction. To clarify this
discrepancy, the authors could strengthen their study by (i) providing a comparative
analysis of S253’s position and function relative to the catalytic Ser residues in classical
triads, and (ii) performing additional mutagenesis, such as S253C or S253T
substitutions, to quantify enzymatic activity and evaluate whether side-chain chemistry
influences catalysis. Such data would help resolve whether S253 is directly catalytic or
plays an auxiliary structural/positioning role in Aur1’s mechanism.
Response: We thank the reviewer for these valuable suggestions. In response, we
generated S253C and S253T mutants and quantitatively compared their enzymatic
activities with those of the wild-type (WT) and S253A variants. Both S253C and S253T
mutants retained substantially higher activity than S253A (Supplementary Fig. 8A),
indicating that S253 is not directly involved in catalysis.
Furthermore, we subsequently compared the active site of Aur1—comprising S253
and the His–His–Asp triad (H255, H294, D298)—with those of representative enzymes
containing a canonical Ser–His–Asp triad, and found no structural equivalence between
them [1-3] (Supplementary Fig. 8B-D). Notably, we found that IPCS Aur1 shares a
conserved LPT fold and conserved His-His-Asp catalytic triad with several canonical
LPT family members [4] (Supplementary Fig. 5, Supplementary Fig. 13). These
enzymes have been proposed to typically rely on a His–His–Asp triad for catalysis,
without the involvement of a serine residue [4-7].
Taken together, our mutagenesis and structural analyses indicate that S253 does not
play a direct catalytic role in Aur1. These findings have been incorporated into the
revised manuscript (Lines 321-328, Page 12).

REVIEWER COMMENTS
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
The manuscript by Hingjun Yu and colleagues describes the cryo-EM structure of the
fungal inositol phosphorylceramide (IPC) synthase from S. cerevisiae, the enzyme
responsible for inositol phosphorylceramide synthesis. IPC is a key component of
fungal membranes, and is absent from mammalian cells. It is therefore an important
anti-fungal drug target. The authors find that IPC synthase is a heterodimer of the Aur1
and Kei1 subunits. The dimer interface is stabilised by a phospholipid and two lipid
alkyl chains. The authors identify H255, H294 and D98 of the Aur1 subunit as being
essential for catalysis and suggest that these three residues form a catalytic triad. A
HHD triad is also found in other fungal IPC synthases despite low sequence similarity.
The authors determined a structure of the complex with the antifungal agent
aureobasidin (AbA) and suggest AbA acts as a competitive inhibitor to block ceramide
binding. Finally, the authors test models of the Aur1-Kei dimer interface, phospholipid
binding and catalysis using mutagenesis.
In general this is an interesting paper. The figures are clear and the cryo-EM work is
sound. Use of the ALFA-binding nanobody to increase size and help alignment was
innovative.
Response: We thank the reviewer for the support and the valuable comments. They are
so helpful to improve our manuscript. We have revised our manuscript accordingly.
1. When describing the structure, the authors do not compare and contrast with other
membrane protein structures. A brief comment on the relatedness of IPC synthase to
other membrane protein structures would be informative and useful, or is this a novel
structure?
Response: We thank the reviewer for this insightful suggestion. In response, we have
added a section comparing the IPC synthase structure with other known membrane
proteins identified by DALI analysis [1]. This analysis not only underscores the
structural novelty of both Aur1 and Kei1 but also reveals a conserved LPT (lipid
phosphatase/phosphotransferase) fold within the catalytic subunit Aur1. The related
description has been incorporated into the revised manuscript (Lines 190-219 on Page
7-8; Supplementary Fig. 5) as follows:
“A DALI server search for the regulatory subunit Kei1 of the IPC heterodimer did not
yield any structurally similar homologs [1]. In contrast, for the catalytic subunit Aur1,
although the overall architecture of Aur1 differs from previously reported structures, a
DALI homology search identified several membrane-protein structures that resemble a
portion of Aur1’s transmembrane topology (residues 143-314) (Supplementary Fig.
5). These include (in a descending order of Z-score): Lipid A 1-Phosphatase (LpxE),
Glucose-6-phosphatase (G6PC1), Phosphatidylglycerophosphatase B (PgpB), and
Sphingomyelin synthase-related protein 1 (SMSr) [2-5]. Despite their low sequence
conservation (<10% identities), structural superposition revealed that a cluster of five
successive transmembrane helices of these proteins adopt comparable topologies,
whereas the remaining regions diverge in both fold and number of transmembrane
helices (Supplementary Fig. 5). Notably, all these structurally related proteins belong
to lipid phosphatase/phosphotransferase (LPT) family, most members of which are
integral membrane enzymes catalyzing the dephosphorylation or phosphotransfer
reactions of diverse phospho-lipid or phospho-carbohydrate substrate [6]. This suggests
that these enzymes (including Aur1, LpxE, G6PC1, PgpB, SMSr) share a conserved
structural module, which we term the LPT fold. This fold exhibits several common
features (Supplementary Fig. 5): it comprises five transmembrane helices, often
situated in the C-terminal region (except in G6PC1); the luminal loop (e.g., EL4 in Aur1)
connecting the last two helices harbors a catalytically essential histidine residue (e.g.,
H294 in Aur1; see Discussions for further mechanistic details). Despite this conserved
core, notable structural variations exist. The orientation and length of the topologically
equivalent transmembrane helices differ among family members. For instance, the first
helix of the module is continuous in SMSr (TM5) but kinked in Aur1 (TM4), LpxE
(TM1), G6PC1 (TM1), and PgpB (TM2), reflecting structural variability within this
shared scaffold (see Discussion for further comparison).”
Notably, this analysis also provides critical clues for elucidating its catalytic
mechanism, as further discussed in our comparative analysis of the active sites in the
revised manuscript (Lines 509-529 on Page 18-19; Supplementary Fig. 13).

3. The authors suggest that the catalytic triad of His255, His294 and Asp298 catalyse
inositol phosphate transfer. A reaction schematic to show the catalytic reaction

Response: We thank the reviewer for this valuable suggestion. Accordingly, we have
added a reaction schematic (Figure 3I) to illustrate the proposed catalytic mechanism
involving the His255-His294-Asp298 triad. The mechanism has been incorporated into
the revised manuscript (Lines 348-355, Page 12-13) as follows:
“We propose a two-step catalytic mechanism for IPC synthesis (Fig. 3I). In the first
step, D298 activates H294 to initiate a nucleophilic attack on the phosphate group of
PI, leading to the formation of an enzyme–phosphoinositol intermediate and the release
of diacylglycerol (DAG). In the second step, H255 activates the hydroxyl group of an
incoming ceramide, which attacks the intermediate and transfers the phosphorylinositol
moiety to ceramide, ultimately forming inositol phosphorylceramide (IPC).”

formation of an enzyme-phosphoinositol intermediate and the release of diacylglycerol
(DAG). In the second step, H255 activates the hydroxyl group of ceramide, which
attacks the enzyme-bound intermediate to generate inositol phosphorylceramide (IPC).
4. Where is the binding site for phosphatidylinositol in Aur1? How is IPC synthase
specific for phosphatidylinositol and not able use phosphatidylcholine (PC) or
phosphatidylethanolamine?
Response: We thank the reviewer for raising these important questions. To address
these points, we performed molecular docking of PI into the Aur1 structure
(Supplementary Fig. 9A). The result indicates that PI occupies the reaction chamber
identified in our ceramide-bound IPCS structure. Specifically, the inositol group of PI
is nestled deep within a pocket formed by transmembrane helices TM5–TM7 and
luminal loops EL3 and EL4 (Supplementary Fig. 9B-C). The shape of this pocket
appears to optimally accommodate the bulkier inositol group of PI (Supplementary
Fig. 9C-D), likely underlying the observed phospholipid preference (Fig. 1C).
Importantly, in this binding pose, the phosphate group of PI is positioned in close
proximity to the catalytically essential residues H255 and H294 (Supplementary Fig.
9D), which is consistent with our proposed reaction mechanism described above (Fig.
3I).
The corresponding descriptions have been incorporated into the revised manuscript
(Lines 334-347, Page 12; Supplementary Fig. 9).

Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
This study presents cryo-EM structures of IPC synthase in complex with its substrate
ceramide and the inhibitor AbA. The authors successfully identified the substrate-
binding cavity and the AbA inhibitor pocket, providing critical insights into the
enzyme’s catalytic mechanism. Complementary biochemical and cell-based assays
robustly validate the essential role of IPC synthase catalytic activity in fungal
sphingolipid biosynthesis. Notably, the resolution of a high-resolution structure for this
~71 kDa membrane protein—achieved through the combination of an ALFA epitope tag
and a high-affinity nanobody—represents a significant methodological advancement in
the field of membrane protein structural biology.
Overall, the topic is of interest given the essential role of IPC synthase in fungal
sphingolipid metabolism and its potential as an antifungal drug target. However, I note
that a closely related study by Wu et al. (Nature Communications, 2025) has already
reported high-resolution structures of the Aur1–Kei1 complex bound to AbA, identifying
the catalytic H–H–D triad, key resistance mutations, and the dimeric architecture.
Therefore, my comments will focus more on the novelty part of this work relative to
Wu’s paper.
Response: We thank the reviewer for the support and the important comments to
improve the manuscript. We have revised our manuscript accordingly.
Major points:
1. A major concern with the current manuscript is the insufficient acknowledgment of
critical related literature. Wu et al. reported cryo-EM structures of the S. cerevisiae
Aur1–Kei1 complex bound to Aureobasidin A, describing the same protein target and
inhibitor, and this work should be explicitly cited in both the Introduction and
Discussion. The authors need to carefully compare their findings with those of Wu et al.
to highlight both consistencies (such as the catalytic H–H–D triad, AbA resistance
mutations, and overall architecture) and differences (including the ceramide-bound
state and lipid-mediated assembly) to avoid overstating novelty.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this important comment. We fully agree that the
study by Wu et al. should be appropriately acknowledged and compared. As
recommended, we have revised the manuscript to explicitly compare our study with
this recently published work and to clarify our unique contributions (see Lines 530-563
on Page 19-20) as mentioned below:
During the preparation of this manuscript, Wu et al. reported the cryo-EM structure
of the S. cerevisiae Aur1–Kei1 IPC synthase complex (IPCS) bound to Aureobasidin A
(AbA) [1]. To overcome challenges posed by the small size of IPCS (~71 kd) and the
absence of prominent soluble domain for particle alignment, these two studies used
distinct strategies. Wu et al. achieved structure determination by imposing C2
symmetry on a dimerized complex, but beyond the AbA-bound form, they were unable
to resolve additional functional states due to the lack of AbA-mediated stabilization [1].
In contrast, we employed an independent approach utilizing an ALFA tag and a
nanobody as fiducial markers (Supplementary Fig. 1), which enabled us to capture
multiple functional states of IPCS, including both the AbA- and ceramide-bound forms
(Fig. 3, Fig. 4).
Despite being determined independently, the structural insights from AbA-bound
states from both studies are in excellent agreement, uncovering consistent overall
architecture, drug-binding site, and mechanisms of drug inhibition and resistance.
Notably, our structural and functional analyses revealed a stabilizing role of lipids at
the Aur1-Kei1 interface (Fig. 2F-J), a feature implicated but not explored in another
study [1].
Beyond these consensus findings, our work provides several unique insights. While
analysis of catalytic mechanism was almost not included in their study, Wu et al.
proposed that Aur1 and SMSr share similar substrate-binding pockets and catalytic
mechanism based on analogy with the substrate-bound SMSr structure [1]. In contrast,
our ceramide-bound Aur1 structure—exclusively obtained in this study—reveals an
adapted reaction chamber and ceramide-binding mode (Supplementary Fig. 12).
Moreover, this divergence also extends to the catalytic mechanism (Supplementary
Fig. 13): while SMSr relies on additional catalytic residues (E205 and D295) absent in
Aur1 and canonical LPT members [2-3], our data supports an alternative mechanism
consistent with that of canonical LPT enzymes (see discussions below for more detailed
comparison between Aur1 and SMSr).
Importantly, by comparing our AbA-bound and ceramide-bound states, we directly
visualize the competitive relationship between substrate and drug (Fig. 4E). This
comparison analysis further captures the conformational dynamics within Aur1,
revealing how AbA binding induces pronounced rearrangements in key drug-
interacting residues and the adjacent TM2–TM3 region (Fig. 4E-F). The exclusive
comparison of multiple functional states advances the molecular insights into AbA
binding and AbA-mediated inhibition.

[1] Wu, X., Gong, X. & Xie, T. Mechanisms of aureobasidin A inhibition and drug
resistance in a fungal IPC synthase complex. Nature Communications 16, 5010 (2025).
[2] Hu, K. et al. Cryo-EM structure of human sphingomyelin synthase and its
mechanistic implications for sphingomyelin synthesis. Nat Struct Mol Biol 31, 884-895
(2024).
[3] Sigal, Y. J., McDermott, M. I. & Morris, A. J. Integral membrane lipid
phosphatases/phosphotransferases: common structure and diverse functions. Biochem
J 387, 281-293 (2005).
In addition, because IPC synthase belongs to the sphingomyelin synthase (SMS) family,
readers would benefit from a broader discussion that integrates previous structural and
biochemical studies on SMS enzymes. Such a comparison could illuminate how the H–
H–D catalytic triad and substrate positioning in IPC synthase relate to SMS enzymes,
and whether conserved or divergent features explain differences in substrate specificity.
Incorporating these key references and analyses will provide proper context, clarify the
unique contributions of the present study, and strengthen its impact.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this insightful suggestion. Following this
comment and a related point from Reviewer 1 (Point #1), we have now incorporated a
thorough comparison between IPC synthase and structural homologs (with low
sequence homologies) identified through DALI analysis [1], including the human
sphingomyelin synthase (SMS) family member-SMSr [2]. This analysis not only
highlights the structural novelty of Aur1 and Kei1 but also identifies a conserved LPT
(lipid phosphatase/phosphotransferase) fold within the catalytic subunit Aur1, offering
key mechanistic clues for understanding its catalytic mechanism (see also our response
to Reviewer 1, Point #1).
Furthermore, in direct response to this suggestion, we have conducted a detailed
comparative analysis between IPCS Aur1 and SMSr [2]. These results help delineate
their conserved and notable divergent features (as described in the revised manuscript
on Lines 488-529, Pages 17–19), as listed below:
(1) Structural comparison between IPCS Aur1 and SMSr:
Despite their limited sequence identity (<10%) between IPCS Aur1 and SMSr,
their
structures can be superimposed with an RMSD of 3.5 Å over 264 aligned residues
(Supplementary Fig. 12A-B). Beyond the conserved LPT fold (Supplementary Fig.
5), TM1 of SMSr can also align with TM3 of Aur1, though the latter become
discontinuous in Aur1. Despite their overall resemblance, key differences emerge near
the reaction chamber (Supplementary Fig. 12C-E). First, in Aur1, TM4—which lines
the side wall of the reaction chamber and corresponds to the continuous TM2 in
SMSr—is interrupted and kinked by a unique ‘Gly-Ala-Pro’ loop. Second, the extended
luminal EL3 loop of Aur1, which caps the reaction chamber, adopts a markedly
different conformation from the corresponding EL2 of SMSr. Consistent with these
structural variations, although ceramide occupies comparable positions within the
reaction chambers, its binding pose differs between the two enzymes. Given their
distinct substrate specificities (PI for Aur1 versus PE for SMSr), it is conceivable that
the structural differences surrounding the reaction chamber may underlie this
divergence, a hypothesis that merits further investigation.
(2) Comparison of the catalytic mechanisms between IPCS Aur1 and SMSr
Consistent with the shared LPT module (Supplementary Fig. 5), detailed structural
comparisons of Aur1 with other LPT members further reveal that the H-H-D catalytic
triad (comprising one histidine from the C2 motif and a histidine-aspartate pair from
the ‘HXXXD’ C3 motif) is conserved and arranged in a remarkably similar spatial
configuration [3] (Supplementary Fig. 13). In particular, the catalytic histidine within
the C3 motif (e.g., H294 in Aur1) is absolutely conserved, suggesting a unified catalytic
mechanism. In our proposed catalytic model for Aur1 (Fig. 3I), the invariant C3
histidine (H294), activated by D298 in the same motif, acts as a nucleophile to form a
transient phosphohistidine intermediate, while the C2 histidine (H255) facilitates
further phosphate transfer. This mechanism is consistent with those established for LPT
enzymes such as LpxE, G6PC1, and PgpB, among others [3-6]. In contrast, SMSr has
been proposed to employ a distinct catalytic strategy, wherein two catalytic residues
(first, C2 histidine H301, activated by E205; second, D295, activated by C3 H344 and
D348) mediates two sequential catalytic steps [2]. It is noted that these additional
catalytic residues in SMSr (E205 and D295) are outside the C2 and C3 motifs and are
not conserved in Aur1 and several LPT members such as LpxE, G6PC1 and PgpB
(Supplementary Fig. 13B-F). These functional distinctions suggest that divergent
catalytic mechanism may occur in the context of conserved H-H-D catalytic triad,
warranting further investigation.

2. The capture of ceramide in the active site is indeed a valuable addition not present
in Wu et al., and the authors support their proposed structural model and catalytic
mechanism with mutagenesis of key residues in the reaction chamber, which resulted in
reduced activity. However, to strengthen this conclusion, they should provide evidence
that the observed effects are not due to global misfolding of the enzyme but rather
specific to the catalytic center—for example, by assessing the stability or expression of
the purified mutant proteins with size-exclusion FPLC.
Moreover, the H157A mutant retains ~50% activity, showing the least impairment
among the catalytic site variants; a brief discussion of why different mutations within
the catalytic center yield varied activity reductions would be helpful.
Finally, it remains uncertain whether the ceramide density reflects a true catalytic
intermediate or a trapped state introduced during purification and exposure to
detergents or exogenous lipids. The authors should discuss the likelihood of ceramide
incorporation under their preparation conditions and address how well this state
represents in vivo substrate binding.
Response: We thank the review for these insightful comments, which have been
addressed accordingly in our revised manuscript.
Regarding the concern about potential misfolding of the mutants, we first verified
that all key mutants were expressed at levels comparable to the wild-type (WT) enzyme,
as shown by western blot analysis (Supplementary Fig. 2C). Furthermore, in direct
response to the reviewer's suggestion, we purified these mutants and assessed their
states by size-exclusion FPLC (Superose 6 Increase 10/300 GL column). The elution
profiles of all mutants were similar to that of the WT complex (Supplementary Fig.
2D), which is consistent with their maintained subunit stoichiometry (Supplementary
Fig. 2B). Together, these data support the proper folding of all mutants analyzed. We
have incorporated these results and corresponding discussion into the revised
manuscript (Lines 312-315, Page 11).
About the varied activity impairment of different catalytic site mutants, it shows a
hierarchy of functional contributions that offers valuable insights into the catalytic
mechanism. Mutations H255A, H294A, and D298A each completely abolished IPC
synthase activity (Fig. 3G-H), supporting them as essential members of the catalytic
triad. In contrast, other active-site mutations (H293A, H157A, and S253A) led to
varying degrees of partial activity loss, with H157A, located farthest from the catalytic
triad, showing the least impairment (~50% residual activity) (Fig. 3G-H). This
gradation in mutational effects suggests that while the catalytic triad (H255, H294,
D298) is indispensable for the core enzymatic reaction, neighboring residues such as
H157, S253, and H293 also contribute to activity. These latter auxiliary residues may
help maintain optimal catalytic geometry, fine-tune substrate orientation, or stabilize
the active-site environment, though their precise mechanistic roles await further
elucidation. We have included a discussion of this interpretation in the revised
manuscript (Lines 315-333, Page 11-12).
About ceramide, following reviewer’s suggestion, we have considered it carefully
and would like to present the following evidence supporting its incorporation and
functional relevance. As detailed in the Methods section (Lines 615-622, Page 22),
ceramide was the only exogenous lipid added throughout the purification procedure for
preparing the ceramide-bound complex. While LMNG (lauryl maltose neopentyl glycol)
and CHS (cholesteryl hemisuccinate) were employed as two essential purification
detergents, the well-defined electron density closely matches the ceramide structure and
cannot be reasonably fitted to either detergent (Supplementary Fig. 4B and 4D):
neither to CHS with a distinct sterol scaffold, nor to LMNG with bulky maltose-based
headgroup that is also sterically incompatible with the narrow, groove-shaped active
site. Importantly, the ceramide headgroup is positioned in proximity to the catalytic
triad, consistent with the proposed reaction mechanism of IPC synthase and canonical
LPT enzymes [1] (Fig. 3D and 3I). Moreover, the bound ceramide conformation
sterically clashes with AbA, suggesting a competitive inhibition mechanism for this
drug (Fig. 4E). Together, these evidences strongly support ceramide incorporation as
well as the functional relevance of the observed ceramide-bound state. We have
included a discussion of this interpretation in the revised manuscript (Lines 287-295,
Page 10-11).
